elements.label: section_header
elements.text: The birth of molecular biology

elements.label: text
elements.text: How biophysicists and biochemists in the 1950s shaped a new science.

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Designs for Life: Molecular Biology After World War II

elements.label: text
elements.text: by Soraya de Chadarevian Cambridge University Press: 2002. 444 pp. £35, $55

elements.label: section_header
elements.text: Vernon M. Ingram

elements.label: text
elements.text: The history of the genesis and development of the molecular-biology group at Cambridge University, UK, under Max Perutz is endlessly fascinating. Why did it begin? Why in Cambridge? Why at that time? And why these particular scientists?

elements.label: text
elements.text: Soraya de Chadarevian presents a historian's account of the conception and birth of the group that founded what is arguably the reigning movement in modern biology. She describes the circumstances and tactics needed to enable the field of molecular biology to mature from a child to become an adolescent, with predictable awkwardness, and then to achieve adulthood. Throughout gestation and childhood it was nurtured by Perutz, who had a clear vision of the next essential step in the development of biological science.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Perutz, who died earlier this year, set out to solve the chemical structure of haemoglobin, the protein molecule that carries oxygen in vertebrates. He took from John Desmond Bernal and Lawrence Bragg the notion that the young science of X-ray crystallography could be used not only to find the chemical structures of small molecules such as salts and sugars, but also the structure of enormously complex molecules such as haemoglobin. Many people told him he was crazy, that the task was impossible; however, he succeeded after some 25 years. De Chadarevian gives a clear account of this story.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Perutz attracted a nucleus of remarkably able young collaborators. His single-minded devotion to the task and his personality were key to this collaboration coming together. There was John Kendrew, who solved the structure of the muscle protein myoglobin; Francis Crick and James Watson, who solved the structure of DNA; Tony Broad, the engineer who made the most powerful X-ray machine in the world; Hugh Huxley, who (with Jean Hanson) solved the molecular mechanism of muscle contraction; and, a little later, Sydney Brenner, who with Crick founded much of modern molecular genetics. I was fortunate to be an early member of the group (1952-58), working as a protein chemist, helping the X-ray crystallographers, and studying the defect caused by the sickle-cellanaemia mutation. Perutz was mentor to the whole group.

elements.label: caption
elements.text: Protein pioneers: (from left) Hugh Huxley, John Kendrew, Max Perutz, Francis Crick, Fred Sanger and Sydney Brenner were the driving force behind the Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The excitement about our work was palpable; it permeated every conversation and dominated our leisure time. However, the book fails to capture this excitement. This is unfortunate, because we were spurred on and held together by an obsessive desire to understand the molecules of life - proteins and nucleic acids. In Designs for Life, the historian eclipses the storyteller.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Also lost is the spirit of intense competitiveness that we felt towards Linus Pauling and his group at the California Institute of Technology, and the X-ray crystallographers at King's College London. Although de Chadarevian gives historical credit to other groups who worked on X-ray crystallography, and protein chemistry in particular, she only touches on the crucial importance of knowing the amino-acid sequences of myoglobin and haemoglobin when progressing from a crude to a detailed structure of these proteins. This information was developed in the United States, and was not available earlier to Perutz and Kendrew.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The early X-ray crystallographers' use of existing and new technologies to solve major biological problems is well described in this book - they were "the right men at the right time". Also fascinating is the crucially important and parallel development of digital computing in the Cambridge University Mathematics Department next door. There was a difference in personality between Perutz and his pupil Kendrew. The latter embraced and spearheaded the development of computers, but he had to be defensively careful about their use because of Perutz's early scepticism about the accuracy of the new method.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Designs for Life deals well with certain important areas of history. The author links the timing of the appearance of the early Medical Research Council (MRC) unit in Cambridge to the availability of new technologies developed during the war in Britain and the United States, and to the availability of young and eager scientists who had had maturing experiences during the Second World War. The early group, led by Perutz, used their success in solving these incredibly difficult structures to publicize the new science of molecular biology by television, radio and newsprint. They encouraged the development of similar research groups elsewhere, and taught molecular biology to a new generation of students from many countries.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Especially detailed is de Chadarevian's account of the politics involved in expanding the group to the size of an institute, large enough to be varied and self-sustaining. The difficulties encountered were both academic and governmental. Although there is much repetition of this theme, there is also a great deal that is interesting.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The group's expansion was helped enormously by the arrival of Fred Sanger, a protein biochemist who went on to win two Nobel prizes - he was the first to establish

elements.text: book reviews

elements.label: text
elements.text: the complete chemical structure of a protein, insulin, and he later invented the current method for sequencing the genome.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In the late 1950s and early 1960s, the vigorous drive to establish new molecularbiology departments was in full swing in the United States but had barely begun in Britain. As a result of the reluctant atmosphere at Cambridge University, the hoped-for expansion did not occur within a university department. There were delays, prevarication and disappointments before the group arrived at their large new MRC site on the outskirts of Cambridge. Unfortunately, this was far away from the university, so the researchers were not integrated into its teaching and collegiality. This enforced separation was in part responsible for the desire of so many of the group to leave the MRC laboratory for teaching positions elsewhere. It is interesting to speculate whether a true integration into Cambridge University would have prevented the exodus.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Much space in this book is devoted to the discovery and worldwide expansion of structural protein biochemistry, and rightly so. It is therefore surprising that less attention is paid to the discovery of the Watson-Crick model of DNA. The impact of their double-helix structure was tremendous and lasted for years. Even more than the great influence of protein-structure determination, the DNA model and its consequences were crucial to fashioning modern molecular biology.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In describing the development of molecular biology, de Chadarevian pays some, but not enough, attention to the vital role of scientists such as Erwin Chargaff, William Cochran, Rosalind Franklin and Linus Pauling, not to mention the other American and French groups. After all, truly great advances in biology are built on the work of others - to give them credit would not diminish the achievements of Watson, Crick and Brenner.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Perhaps de Chadarevian should have paid more attention to the influence of Crick and Brenner on the development of the new and exciting fields of molecular genetics and protein synthesis. Their work and the publicizing of their ideas made molecular biology the lingua franca of modern biology. Even the new generation of engineers feel the urgent need to learn this new treatment of biology.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The author deliberately focuses on the (unique) instance of the MRC Unit for the Molecular Structure of Biological Systems, housed in the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, and its direct descendant, the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology. The account of these units' relationship to government, to private funding agencies and to the university makes an interesting and valuable book. One must realize, however, that the narrow focus does not imply that the group was entirely self-contained - we depended, at the time, on the outside world for scientific nourishment and for funding. In short, de Chadarevian's historical account is recommended to all who are interested in the development of molecular biology. ■ Vernon M. Ingram is in the Department of Technology, Massachusetts Institute of Biology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, USA.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Look at Scientific Evidence

elements.label: text

elements.label: text
elements.text: Oxford University Press: 2002. 344 pp. $29.95

elements.label: text
elements.text: Raphael Mechoulam

elements.label: text
elements.text: There seems to be an insatiable appetite for

elements.label: text
elements.text: information on marijuana. The 'books in

elements.label: text
elements.text: print' file on my computer lists 416 books

elements.label: text
elements.text: under 'marijuana', for example. Is such a

elements.label: text
elements.text: deluge justified? Probably not. Does this

elements.label: text
elements.text: book by Mitch Earleywine merely add to it,

elements.label: text
elements.text: or is it really, as the subtitle claims, a "new

elements.label: text
elements.text: look" at the scientific evidence? It certainly

elements.label: text
elements.text: brings together a considerable amount of

elements.label: text
elements.text: information on cannabis in many fields, and

elements.label: text
elements.text: does so very well, but a new look it is not.

elements.label: text
elements.text: In the past two decades there has been a

elements.label: text
elements.text: renaissance in cannabis research, mostly in

elements.label: text
elements.text: chemistry and biology. Cannabinoid recep-

elements.label: text
elements.text: tors have been identified and endogenous

elements.label: text
elements.text: cannabinoids have been isolated from the

elements.label: text
elements.text: brain and the periphery. The endocannabin-

elements.label: text
elements.text: oids have been found to take part in pro-

elements.label: text
elements.text: cesses in almost all of the major physiological

elements.label: text
elements.text: systems. Most of the work has focused on the

elements.label: text
elements.text: nervous system, but there have been advances

elements.label: text
elements.text: in our understanding of their role in the

elements.label: text
elements.text: immune, reproductive, cardiovascular and

elements.label: text
elements.text: digestive systems. Memory, pain, inflam-

elements.label: text
elements.text: mation, appetite and suckling are some of the physiological processes in which cannabinoids are involved. By contrast, most other aspects have been sadly neglected.

elements.label: text
elements.text: The endogenous cannabinoids, although

elements.label: text
elements.text: now known about for about a decade, have

elements.label: text
elements.text: never been administered to healthy human

elements.label: text
elements.text: beings, let alone patients. Can we compare

elements.label: text
elements.text: this snail's pace with that witnessed with the

elements.label: text
elements.text: hormones insulin and cortisone, for exam-

elements.label: text
elements.text: ple, when, decades ago, clinical research led

elements.label: text
elements.text: to major advances in therapeutics within

elements.label: text
elements.text: months of their discovery? The only

elements.label: text
elements.text: cannabinoid drugs on the market are delta-

elements.label: text
elements.text: 9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the psycho-

elements.label: text
elements.text: active constituent of cannabis, and nabilone,

elements.label: text
elements.text: a more active synthetic drug with a similar

elements.label: text
elements.text: profile. Both were introduced about 15 years

elements.label: text
elements.text: ago. Even cannabidiol, a non-psychoactive,

elements.label: text
elements.text: non-toxic cannabis constituent with known

elements.label: text
elements.text: anti-oxidative, anti-inflammatory, anti-

elements.label: text
elements.text: nausea and anti-epileptic properties, has

elements.label: text
elements.text: yet to be adequately evaluated in patients.

elements.label: text
elements.text: This deplorable situation has hampered

elements.label: text
elements.text: advances in many fields, particularly in

elements.label: text
elements.text: psychology. There is a limit to what animal

elements.label: text
elements.text: work can teach us about human emotions,

elements.label: text
elements.text: cognition and behaviour. Until we learn

elements.label: text
elements.text: more about the endocannabinoid system in

elements.label: text
elements.text: humans, a "new look" at the field is bound

elements.label: text
elements.text: to be premature.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Two years ago, Oxford University Press

elements.label: text
elements.text: published The Science of Marijuanaby Leslie

elements.label: text
elements.text: Iversen (for a review, see Nature 407, 18-19;

elements.label: text
elements.text: 2000), an excellent book in which the

elements.label: text
elements.text: emphasis is on the biological aspects and

elements.label: text
elements.text: medical uses of marijuana. Earleywine, on

elements.label: text
elements.text: the other hand, while also addressing these

elements.label: text
elements.text: aspects, devotes most of his book to the psy-

elements.label: text
elements.text: chological and social aspects of marijuana

elements.label: text
elements.text: use. Unfortunately, these aspects have not

elements.label: text
elements.text: been part of the scientific renaissance of

elements.label: text
elements.text: recent years. Although the available material

elements.label: text
elements.text: is thoughtfully and critically discussed, I was

elements.label: text
elements.text: left with a feeling of déjà vu.

elements.label: text
elements.text: Earleywine, as befits a clinical psycholo-

elements.label: text
elements.text: gist, believes in both statistics and common
